data.title: Rows and variables
data.prompt: A table has 5 units and 3 variables. One unit is removed and one variable is added. How many units and how many variables remain?
data.answer: Four units and four variables remain.

data.title: A mean is not the data
data.prompt: A paper reports only that the mean of ten heights is 170 cm. How many recorded heights are in that sentence?
data.answer: None. The sentence reports a summary. The ten heights are the data, and they are not shown.

dataset.title: Relative frequency after a deletion
dataset.prompt: The dataset of household sizes is 2, 4, 3, 2, 5. The household of size 5 is removed. What is the relative frequency of the value 2?
dataset.answer: The value 2 appears twice among the four remaining sizes, so the relative frequency is 2/4 = 1/2.

dataset.title: Mean of what remains
dataset.prompt: Using the same reduced dataset 2, 4, 3, 2, what is the mean?
dataset.answer: The total is 11 and there are 4 observations, so the mean is 11/4 = 2.75.

variable.title: Frequency of a category
variable.prompt: Six animals have species cat, dog, cat, cat, dog, rabbit. A seventh animal is a cat. How many cats are there?

variable.title: A code is not a mean of the category
variable.prompt: Pain is coded 1, 2, 3 for none, mild, and severe. The codes of three patients are 1, 3, and 2. Why is the average 2 not a pain?
variable.answer: The codes name ordered categories. Their average is an average of codes, not a pain on that scale.

levels-of-measurement.title: Mean of scores
levels-of-measurement.prompt: Five test scores are 90, 70, 80, 95, and 70. A sixth score of 85 is added. What is the mean of the six scores?
levels-of-measurement.answer: The total is 405 + 85 = 490. The mean is 490/6.

levels-of-measurement.title: Frequency of a grade
levels-of-measurement.prompt: Grades A, C, B, A, C are followed by one more grade B. How many times does B appear?

population.title: A new unit
population.prompt: Five workshops have outputs 10, 12, 14, 16, and 18. A sixth workshop with output 20 is added. What is the population mean?
population.answer: The total is 90 over 6 workshops, so the mean is 15.

population.title: A sample that does not change
population.prompt: In that same population, a sample of the two smallest outputs, 10 and 12, is kept after the sixth workshop is added. What is the sample mean?

sample.title: Enlarging a sample
sample.prompt: Population values are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. The sample 2, 4, 6 is enlarged by the value 8. What is the new sample mean?
sample.answer: The sample values are 2, 4, 6, and 8. Their mean is 5.

sample.title: The population mean
sample.prompt: For the population 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, what is the population mean after that sample is enlarged?
sample.answer: The population is unchanged, so its mean remains 6.

census.title: Census mean of ten
census.prompt: Eight outputs sum to 50. Two more outputs, 7 and 9, are added and every workshop is observed. What is the census mean?
census.answer: The total is 66 over 10 workshops, so the mean is 6.6.

census.title: A sample that stays put
census.prompt: A sample of three outputs 5, 8, and 4 is not enlarged when those two workshops are added. What is the sample mean?

parameter.title: A new population mean
parameter.prompt: The values 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 are the whole population. A sixth value 16 is added to the population. What is the new population mean?
parameter.answer: The total is 46 over 6 values, so the mean is 46/6 = 23/3.

parameter.title: The statistic does not follow
parameter.prompt: The sample stays 2, 4, 6 after that sixth population value is added. What is the sample mean?

sampling-distribution.title: Expectation of the sample mean
sampling-distribution.prompt: From the population 1, 2, 3, the equally likely sample means of size 2 are 1.5, 2, and 2.5. What is their expectation?

sampling-distribution.title: Samples of size one
sampling-distribution.prompt: Samples of size 1 from 1, 2, 3 are equally likely. What is the expectation of that sampling distribution?

line-chart.title: A new household
line-chart.prompt: Sizes 2, 2, 3, 4, 2 gain one more household of size 3. What is the absolute frequency of 3?

line-chart.title: Relative frequency of 2
line-chart.prompt: After that addition there are six households and the value 2 still appears three times. What is the relative frequency of 2?

abundance-estimation.title: A second sample with no marks
abundance-estimation.prompt: Why does the Petersen estimator give no finite population size when the second sample contains no marked animals?
abundance-estimation.answer: The estimator divides by the recapture count, so a recapture count of zero leaves the ratio undefined.

abundance-estimation.title: Closure
abundance-estimation.prompt: What must be negligible between the two samples if the Petersen estimator is to refer to the population size at marking?
abundance-estimation.answer: Births, deaths, and movement must be negligible, so the population is closed over that interval.

abundance-estimation.title: When the small-sample form is the one to use
abundance-estimation.prompt: Krebs describes the Chapman form as nearly unbiased once how many recaptures have been seen?

apriori-algorithm.title: Skipping a candidate
apriori-algorithm.prompt: Why may a candidate item set be left uncounted when one of its subsets failed the support threshold?
apriori-algorithm.answer: Support cannot rise when an item is added, so a set that contains an infrequent subset is infrequent.

apriori-algorithm.title: Lift below one
apriori-algorithm.prompt: What does a lift below 1 say about the two items in the baskets that were counted?
apriori-algorithm.answer: They occur together less often than the product of their separate supports.

apriori-algorithm.title: Confidence and support
apriori-algorithm.prompt: Why can a rule have high confidence while its item set still fails a support threshold?
apriori-algorithm.answer: Confidence is the fraction of antecedent baskets that also contain the consequent, while support is the fraction of all baskets that contain the pair.

average-treatment-effect.title: A null average
average-treatment-effect.prompt: What does an average treatment effect of zero say about the two potential-outcome means?
average-treatment-effect.answer: The population means under the two actions are equal.

average-treatment-effect.title: The missing column
average-treatment-effect.prompt: Why can the average treatment effect not be computed by subtracting the two outcomes inside each person's observed row?
average-treatment-effect.answer: Only one of the two potential outcomes is observed for each person.

average-treatment-effect.title: Difference and ratio
average-treatment-effect.prompt: A risk of 0.2 under treatment and 0.3 under the comparison is a risk difference of what?

base-rate.title: Which factor it is
base-rate.prompt: In the positive predictive value, which probability is the base rate?
base-rate.answer: It is the probability of the condition before the test result is known.

base-rate.title: Raising the base rate
base-rate.prompt: If the sensitivity exceeds the false-positive rate, how does the positive predictive value move when the base rate rises?

base-rate.title: A sensitive test and a rare condition
base-rate.prompt: Why can a sensitive test still have a small positive predictive value?
base-rate.answer: When the condition is rare, false positives from the large unaffected group can outnumber true positives.

bayesian-inference.title: The factor that cancels
bayesian-inference.prompt: In the posterior odds between two parameter values, which factor from Bayes' theorem does not need to be computed?
bayesian-inference.answer: The marginal probability of the data, because it is the same for both values and cancels.

bayesian-inference.title: A further observation
bayesian-inference.prompt: When a new observation arrives, what may be used as its prior so that the result matches conditioning on the combined sample?
bayesian-inference.answer: The posterior from the observations already in hand.

bayesian-model.title: The two factors
bayesian-model.prompt: Name the two factors in the joint distribution of a Bayesian model.
bayesian-model.answer: The prior distribution of the unknowns and the sampling distribution of the data given the unknowns.

bayesian-model.title: An improper function
bayesian-model.prompt: Why does a function of the unknown whose integral diverges fail to complete a joint probability model?
bayesian-model.answer: It is not a probability distribution for the unknown, so the joint distribution is not defined as a probability.

bayesian-probability.title: Coherence
bayesian-probability.prompt: What does coherence require of a set of betting prices?
bayesian-probability.answer: No combination of bets should win for sure from the person who posted the prices, and the prices then satisfy the probability axioms.

bayesian-probability.title: A parameter and a draw
bayesian-probability.prompt: Does assigning a Bayesian probability to a parameter, by itself, mean the parameter was drawn from a population of parameters?
bayesian-probability.answer: No. That reading is a hierarchical model. The probability is a degree of uncertainty about the parameter.

case-control-study.title: The sample fraction of cases
case-control-study.prompt: Why does the proportion of the sample who are cases not estimate the population risk?
case-control-study.answer: The design fixes how many cases and how many controls are included.

case-control-study.title: The contrast the design supports
case-control-study.prompt: When the controls represent the source population's exposure distribution, which contrast does the design estimate?

causality.title: The outcome that was seen
causality.prompt: If a person received treatment A = a, which potential outcome equals the observed outcome?
causality.answer: The potential outcome under action a.

causality.title: When the two contrasts agree
causality.prompt: Under what design condition do the associational contrast and the causal contrast agree?
causality.answer: When the groups receiving the two treatments are exchangeable, which is what random assignment is designed to produce.

censoring-statistics.title: Which quantity is fixed
censoring-statistics.prompt: In Type I censoring, which of the stopping time and the number of failures is fixed before the test is run?
censoring-statistics.answer: The stopping time is fixed. The number of failures is random.

censoring-statistics.title: A removed unit
censoring-statistics.prompt: Does a unit removed without failure create its own multiplicative drop in the product-limit estimator?
censoring-statistics.answer: No. It stays in the risk set only until the last failure before removal, and it is omitted afterwards without a failure factor of its own.

classification.title: Equal costs
classification.prompt: The Bayes classifier picks the class with the largest conditional probability when every mistake has the same cost. If missing one class is much more costly than missing another, does that same ordering still pick the action?
classification.answer: No. The probability ordering is the right ordering only under equal misclassification costs. A higher cost on one mistake can make a less probable class the better announcement.

classification.title: Training match
classification.prompt: A rule labels every training case correctly. What does that match say about the conditional error at a new feature value where the classes still overlap?
classification.answer: Nothing that removes the overlap. The conditional error at the new value is the probability left over after the best label, and a perfect training match is an answer to a different question.

classification.title: Logistic regression
classification.prompt: Why is logistic regression a classification method even though its name says regression?
classification.answer: The response is qualitative. The fitted object is a class probability, and the label is read off that probability.

cluster-analysis.title: Two starts
cluster-analysis.prompt: Why can two runs of K-means on the same points return different within-cluster sums of squares?
cluster-analysis.answer: The alternating assignment of points to centres stops at a local minimum. A different start can reach a different partition.

cluster-analysis.title: Choosing K
cluster-analysis.prompt: Why is cross-validation of a prediction error not a way to choose the number of clusters?
cluster-analysis.answer: There is no response to predict, so there is no prediction error to cross-validate. A smaller within-cluster sum of squares at a larger number of centres can just mean the extra centre split one cloud.

cluster-analysis.title: Single linkage
cluster-analysis.prompt: Single linkage and complete linkage use the same pairwise distances. What is the only change between them?
cluster-analysis.answer: Single linkage takes the minimum pairwise distance between groups. Complete linkage takes the maximum.

cohort-study.title: A risk needs a denominator
cohort-study.prompt: Why can a cohort yield a risk when a case-control sample of the same disease cannot?
cohort-study.answer: Cohort membership is fixed before the outcome is used to select people, so the proportion who develop the outcome is a risk in that cohort. A case-control sample chooses cases and non-cases in proportions the investigator sets, so that proportion is not the risk.

cohort-study.title: Follow-up is not assignment
cohort-study.prompt: People are followed forward and the exposed have a higher risk than the unexposed. What further condition is needed before that difference is read as an effect of the exposure?
cohort-study.answer: The exposed and unexposed have to be comparable apart from the exposure, or an adjustment has to be believed to make them so. Follow-up alone does not assign the exposure.

conjoint-analysis.title: Importance and the design
conjoint-analysis.prompt: Why is a part-worth range an importance only relative to the levels that were shown?
conjoint-analysis.answer: The range is the difference between the part-worths of the levels included in the design. A different set of levels changes the range, so the share is not a property of the attribute in the abstract.

conjoint-analysis.title: Ranks and least squares
conjoint-analysis.prompt: Why can ordinary least squares be a poor match to rank data even when the recovered numbers look similar?
conjoint-analysis.answer: Ranks supply an order. Ordinary least squares treats the scores as interval-scaled, which the rank task did not provide. Ordinal methods are a separate class of estimator from interval-scaled regression.

conjoint-analysis.title: Holdouts
conjoint-analysis.prompt: A respondent scores holdout cards that were withheld from the fit, and the sums predict those cards. What does that success not show?
conjoint-analysis.answer: It does not show that the same person would buy the product in a shop. A holdout that repeats the task speaks to forecasting accuracy under the same conditions.

control-group.title: A treated control
control-group.prompt: The control arm quietly receives a version of the experimental treatment. Which contrast does the trial then answer?
control-group.answer: The contrast is between two versions of treatment, not between the experimental treatment and its absence.

control-group.title: Who asks for treatment
control-group.prompt: The untreated set is whoever did not ask for the treatment. Why is that set not yet a control group for an effect?
control-group.answer: Membership follows the request, which can share causes with the outcome. Random assignment is what makes membership unpredictable from those traits.

correlation-does-not-imply-causation.title: Precision is not causation
correlation-does-not-imply-causation.prompt: A larger sample makes an observational association more precise. What does that precision not do?
correlation-does-not-imply-causation.answer: It does not turn the association into a causal effect. The conditional risk and the counterfactual risk remain different contrasts.

correlation-does-not-imply-causation.title: Same ratio, different cases
correlation-does-not-imply-causation.prompt: Why can a relative risk of 2 correspond to very different numbers of cases removed if the exposure is taken away?
correlation-does-not-imply-causation.answer: A small risk against half that risk, and a large risk against half that risk, have the same ratio. The absolute number of cases depends on the level of the risk, not only on the ratio.

correlation-does-not-imply-causation.title: Time order
correlation-does-not-imply-causation.prompt: A factor is measured after the outcome. Why can it not be the cause of that outcome?
correlation-does-not-imply-causation.answer: A cause has to precede the effect. A measurement taken after the outcome fails that time order.

cross-sectional-data.title: Same spreadsheet, different index
cross-sectional-data.prompt: Three annual totals for one country and three countries in one year can look alike in a spreadsheet. Which layout has a within-unit change?
cross-sectional-data.answer: The three annual totals are a time series, so a change from one year to the next is defined. The three countries in one year are a cross-section, and no within-country change is in the table.

cross-sectional-data.title: A regional policy
cross-sectional-data.prompt: A policy is constant inside each of twenty regions and is estimated from thousands of people. Why is the people-count a poor description of the information about that policy?
cross-sectional-data.answer: The policy does not vary inside a region, so the independent contrasts are closer to the number of regions than to the number of people. Default standard errors that ignore the cluster overstate precision.

data-collection.title: A calculated sampling error
data-collection.prompt: A large convenience collection and a small probability sample both produce rows. Which one supports a calculated sampling error, and why?
data-collection.answer: The probability sample, because the selection probabilities are known. A convenience collection does not supply those probabilities.

data-collection.title: The right rows
data-collection.prompt: Why does storing a variable carefully not make it the right variable for a stated question?
data-collection.answer: The collection has to record the quantities the question names. Relevance is fixed by the question, not by the care of the storage.

data-quality.title: Agreement is not accuracy
data-quality.prompt: Repeated readings agree with each other and all sit on the same side of the reference value. Which of precision and accuracy fails?
data-quality.answer: Precision can be fine, because the readings agree. Accuracy fails because of the systematic offset from the reference value. Bias does not affect precision, and accuracy gets worse as bias grows.

data-quality.title: A short frame
data-quality.prompt: Why does a larger sample from a frame that omits a class of units not repair coverage?
data-quality.answer: Coverage error is a property of the frame. Drawing more units from the same frame repeats the omission.

decision-problem.title: A test that changes nothing
decision-problem.prompt: A diagnostic test leaves the preferred treatment unchanged whichever result appears. What is the decision value of the test under expected utility, apart from harm the test itself causes?
decision-problem.answer: It has none. Information changes the expected score only when it changes a later action.

decision-problem.title: Quadratic loss
decision-problem.prompt: Under quadratic loss for a point estimate of a parameter, which summary of the distribution of the parameter minimises the expected loss?

decision-problem.title: The most probable state
decision-problem.prompt: Why is the action with the highest probability of the best state not automatically the solution of a decision problem?
decision-problem.answer: The solution maximises expected utility, or minimises expected loss. An action that sometimes fails can still win if the score, averaged over the outcomes, is better.

difference-in-differences.title: The early gap
difference-in-differences.prompt: The pre-treatment gap between the groups is large. Why is that gap not evidence that the treatment was already working?
difference-in-differences.answer: The treatment was not yet available, so it cannot have caused the earlier measurement. The gap measures confounding.

difference-in-differences.title: Diverging groups
difference-in-differences.prompt: The groups are diverging for reasons that change between the two waves. Which identifying assumption does that break?
difference-in-differences.answer: Additive equi-confounding. The comparison group's change is then not the change the treated group would have had without treatment.

differential-privacy.title: An exact count
differential-privacy.prompt: Why does publishing the exact count of a binary attribute fail pure differential privacy?
differential-privacy.answer: Neighbouring files produce counts that differ by one, so an output with probability 1 on one file has probability 0 on the other. No finite factor e to the epsilon bounds that ratio.

differential-privacy.title: A test of membership
differential-privacy.prompt: A release is alpha-differentially private. A level-gamma test based only on the release asks whether a named subject is in the file. How does alpha limit the power?
differential-privacy.answer: The power is at most gamma times e to the alpha. The test cannot separate the two neighbouring files by more than that factor.

differential-privacy.title: A later summary
differential-privacy.prompt: An analyst maps a differentially private release to a new summary without looking at the private file. What happens to the privacy parameters?
differential-privacy.answer: The mapped release remains differentially private with the same epsilon and delta. The mapping does not spend an additional privacy budget.

dimensionality-reduction.title: Sum of squares
dimensionality-reduction.prompt: The centred points are (-1,-1), (0,0) and (1,1). What is the total sum of squares?
dimensionality-reduction.answer: The total sum of squares is 4.

dimensionality-reduction.title: Horizontal fraction
dimensionality-reduction.prompt: If only the horizontal coordinate of those centred points is kept, what fraction of the sum of squares is retained?

dimensionality-reduction.title: Discarded sum of squares
dimensionality-reduction.prompt: What sum of squares is discarded by keeping only the horizontal coordinate?
dimensionality-reduction.answer: The discarded sum of squares is 2.

diversity-index.title: Concentration of 6, 3, and 1
diversity-index.prompt: Proportions 0.6, 0.3, and 0.1. What is Simpson's λ?

diversity-index.title: Unbiased pair estimator
diversity-index.prompt: Counts 6, 3, and 1. What is the unbiased estimator ℓ?

diversity-index.title: Equal split
diversity-index.prompt: Ten individuals split five and five. What is λ?

effect-size.title: Critical difference
effect-size.prompt: A standard error is 1.7 mmHg. What is 1.96 times that standard error?

effect-size.title: Shifted z-score
effect-size.prompt: The lower critical point is -3.332 and the true difference is -3, with standard error 1.7. What is the z-score?
effect-size.answer: The z-score is about -0.195, which rounds to -0.20.

effect-size.title: A larger effect
effect-size.prompt: The standard error is 2 mmHg and the true difference is -5. Using the critical value 1.96 times 2, what is the z-score of the lower critical point?

estimating-equations.title: Sample mean
estimating-equations.prompt: Observations 2, 4, and 6. What solves the sum of (y minus mu) equals 0?

estimating-equations.title: A second sample
estimating-equations.prompt: Observations 1, 3, and 8. What solves the same estimating equation?

estimating-equations.title: A second moment
estimating-equations.prompt: At mu = 4 for observations 1, 3, and 8, is the average of y squared minus (mu squared + 1) equal to zero?
estimating-equations.answer: No. The average is 74/3 minus 17, about 7.667.

expected-loss.title: Two averages
expected-loss.prompt: Expected loss and the risk of a procedure are both averages of a loss. What is being averaged in each case?
expected-loss.answer: Expected loss averages the loss of one action over the outcomes still uncertain when the action is chosen. The risk averages the loss of a procedure over repeated samples at a fixed parameter.

expected-loss.title: A measurement branch
expected-loss.prompt: Why is the expected loss of measure-then-remediate-if-high the wrong score for a household that will remediate whatever the reading is?
expected-loss.answer: That expectation uses the action taken after the measurement. A household that ignores the reading is taking a different action, so it has a different expected loss.

expected-loss.title: A quadratic report
expected-loss.prompt: A point report about a parameter is scored by squared error under the distribution calculated for the parameter. Which summary minimises the expected loss?
expected-loss.answer: The mean of that distribution, when the mean exists.

experimental-error.title: Two treatments
experimental-error.prompt: Observations (3,5) and (8,10) have treatment means 4 and 9 and grand mean 6.5. What are the treatment and error sums of squares?
experimental-error.answer: The treatment sum of squares is 25 and the error sum of squares is 4.

experimental-error.title: Error mean square
experimental-error.prompt: The error sum of squares is 4 on 2 degrees of freedom. What is the error mean square?

experimental-error.title: A second split
experimental-error.prompt: Observations (1,3) and (5,7) have means 2 and 6 and grand mean 4. What are the two sums of squares?
experimental-error.answer: The treatment sum of squares is 16 and the error sum of squares is 4.

extrapolation.title: Negative aid
extrapolation.prompt: Using aid = 24319 - 0.0431 times income, what aid does an income of 1000000 produce?

extrapolation.title: Inside a larger income
extrapolation.prompt: Using the same line, what aid does an income of 200000 produce?

extrapolation.title: Four hundred thousand
extrapolation.prompt: Using the same line, what aid does an income of 400000 produce?

fat-tails.title: Two samples of five
fat-tails.prompt: Using divisor n, what are the moment kurtoses of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and of 1, 1, 1, 1, 6?
fat-tails.answer: The first kurtosis is 1.7 and the second is 3.25.

fat-tails.title: An exponential tail
fat-tails.prompt: For a unit exponential, what is the probability of exceeding 4, to six decimals, and what is the kurtosis of the law?
fat-tails.answer: The probability is 0.018316 and the kurtosis is 9.

fat-tails.title: Excess over the normal
fat-tails.prompt: A unit exponential has kurtosis 9. What is the excess over the normal value 3, and what is the survival past 1?
fat-tails.answer: The excess is 6. The survival past 1 is about 0.367879.

feature-selection.title: Intercept-only residual sum of squares
feature-selection.prompt: For the cases (x, z, y) = (0, 0, 1), (1, 0, 1) and (2, 1, 3), what is the residual sum of squares of the intercept-only fit?
feature-selection.answer: The residual sum of squares is 8/3.

feature-selection.title: Predictor x alone
feature-selection.prompt: On the same three cases, what is the residual sum of squares of the least-squares line that uses only x and an intercept?
feature-selection.answer: The residual sum of squares is 2/3.

feature-selection.title: How many best-subset models
feature-selection.prompt: Best-subset selection with 20 predictors fits how many models, and forward stepwise fits how many?
feature-selection.answer: Best subset fits 1048576 models. Forward stepwise fits 211.

federated-learning.title: Pooled mean
federated-learning.prompt: One site has values 1 and 3. Another has the single value 10. What is the pooled mean?

federated-learning.title: Unweighted gap
federated-learning.prompt: How much larger is the unweighted mean of the two site means than that pooled mean?

federated-learning.title: Equal sizes
federated-learning.prompt: If the second site instead has two values, both 10, what is the pooled mean?

first-international-statistical-congress.title: Unlike tables
first-international-statistical-congress.prompt: Two offices publish rates whose events or populations were defined differently. Why can the difference of the rates fail to estimate a change in one population?
first-international-statistical-congress.answer: The subtraction mixes unlike events or unlike populations, so it describes the two tables rather than one population observed under a shared definition.

first-international-statistical-congress.title: A centre in each state
first-international-statistical-congress.prompt: What institution did the Brussels programme ask each state to maintain, and what was it supposed to exchange?
first-international-statistical-congress.answer: A central statistical commission, which would exchange publications and the schedules used to collect information.

first-international-statistical-congress.title: A programme, not a completed reform
first-international-statistical-congress.prompt: Why does the end of the congress series in 1876 block a reading of a Brussels resolution as a completed reform of later national tables?
first-international-statistical-congress.answer: No further congress of the series met, so a resolution stayed a programme. Later national tables were not thereby shown to have adopted it.

game-of-chance.title: Euro die
game-of-chance.prompt: A fair die pays 1 on an even face, 2 on a 1 or a 3, and -3 on a 5. What is the expected payoff?

game-of-chance.title: Face value
game-of-chance.prompt: A fair die is scored by the face that appears. What is the expected score, and what is the probability that the face is at most 4?
game-of-chance.answer: The expected score is 21/6 = 3.5. The probability is 4/6 = 2/3.

game-of-chance.title: Wheel
game-of-chance.prompt: A wheel pays 4 with probability 1/4, 0 with probability 1/2, and -2 with probability 1/4. What is the expected payoff?
game-of-chance.answer: The expectation is 1/2, so the game is not fair.

harking.title: Induction and reporting
harking.prompt: A discussion says the data suggested an age split that was not planned. An introduction says the study was designed to test that age split. Which report is HARKing?
harking.answer: The introduction that presents the post hoc split as the hypothesis the study was designed to test. Saying the data suggested the split labels the split as post hoc.

harking.title: A search and a tail
harking.prompt: Twenty true nulls are tested and the smallest p-value is published as if it had been the only pre-specified test. Which error rate is misstated?
harking.answer: The type I error of the published comparison is the error rate of the search, not the error rate of one pre-specified test.

harking.title: A plan
harking.prompt: A comparison was not listed in the pre-analysis plan, and the authors still want to show it. How should it be reported?
harking.answer: As an exploratory result, so a reader can tell it was not the hypothesis fixed before the outcomes were inspected.

harmonic-mean.title: Three interest rates
harmonic-mean.prompt: Rates of 5%, 10% and 15% produce the same income. What is the harmonic mean, as an exact fraction, and what is the arithmetic mean?
harmonic-mean.answer: The harmonic mean is 90/11 percent, about 8.182. The arithmetic mean is 10 percent.

harmonic-mean.title: Three weights
harmonic-mean.prompt: Person weights are 100, 200 and 300. What is the exact harmonic mean, and what integer does it round to?
harmonic-mean.answer: The exact value is 1800/11, about 163.636, which rounds to 164.

harmonic-mean.title: A zero
harmonic-mean.prompt: One of six positive observations is replaced by zero. What happens to the harmonic mean?
harmonic-mean.answer: The harmonic mean is undefined, because a reciprocal of zero is not a number.

hawthorne-effect.title: A room that left
hawthorne-effect.prompt: Output also rose in rooms that were no longer under experimental variation. What does that do to a reading that attributes the studied room's rise only to being studied?
hawthorne-effect.answer: The rise is shared with rooms outside the experiment, so it cannot be read as a response that only the studied room produced.

hawthorne-effect.title: Unchanged Mondays
hawthorne-effect.prompt: Mondays on which the light was not changed show the same within-week output pattern as Mondays on which it was changed. Why does that block a lighting-effect reading of the Monday jump?
hawthorne-effect.answer: The jump appears whether or not the light changed, so the Monday pattern is not identified as an effect of the lighting change.

hawthorne-effect.title: Finer time terms
hawthorne-effect.prompt: A 3 to 4 percent elevation during active experimentation disappeared once room-by-month terms were added. What does that say about an abrupt on/off effect of being studied?
hawthorne-effect.answer: The contrast is not robust to those time controls, so the records do not show an abrupt jump when experimentation is switched on or off.

instrumental-variable.title: Which condition is checked
instrumental-variable.prompt: Of the three instrumental conditions, which one can be verified from the association in the data?
instrumental-variable.answer: The association between the instrument and the treatment. The exclusion restriction and the absence of shared causes stay assumptions.

instrumental-variable.title: A small denominator
instrumental-variable.prompt: Why does a first-stage difference near zero make the Wald ratio unstable?
instrumental-variable.answer: The ratio divides by that difference, so a small denominator inflates the assignment effect and makes the estimate sensitive to small changes in how strongly the instrument moves treatment.

instrumental-variable.title: A fourth condition
instrumental-variable.prompt: The three instrumental conditions hold. Does the Wald ratio equal the average treatment effect?
instrumental-variable.answer: Not from those three conditions alone. A fourth homogeneity condition is required for that reading. Without it the instrument identifies bounds.

inverse-probability.title: One success
inverse-probability.prompt: One trial is a success and the unknown chance is uniform on the unit interval. What is the posterior probability that the chance exceeds 1/2?

inverse-probability.title: One failure
inverse-probability.prompt: One trial is a failure and the unknown chance is uniform on the unit interval. What is the posterior probability that the chance exceeds 1/2?

k-anonymity.title: Minimum frequency
k-anonymity.prompt: Three rows share one quasi-identifier pair and one row has a different pair. What is the minimum frequency?
k-anonymity.answer: The minimum frequency is 1, so the table is not 2-anonymous.

k-anonymity.title: After one added row
k-anonymity.prompt: A second row with the rare pair is added. What is the minimum frequency, and is the table 2-anonymous?
k-anonymity.answer: The minimum frequency is 2, so the table satisfies 2-anonymity.

kruskal-wallis-test.title: Valid rank sums
kruskal-wallis-test.prompt: Three groups of four have rank sums 10, 26, and 42. What is H?

kruskal-wallis-test.title: An impossible sum
kruskal-wallis-test.prompt: Why can the rank sums 12, 24, and 48 not occur for three groups of four on ranks 1 through 12?
kruskal-wallis-test.answer: Those ranks sum to 78, not 84, and a group of four sums to at most 42, so 48 is impossible.

kruskal-wallis-test.title: One-sided rejection
kruskal-wallis-test.prompt: The oil statistic is 13.64 and the chi-squared 5 percent reference with 3 degrees of freedom is 7.81. Does the test reject, and why is a small H not a rejection?
kruskal-wallis-test.answer: Yes, because 13.64 is greater than 7.81. The rejection region contains only large H, because H measures unevenness of the rank sums.

kurtosis.title: A short flat sample
kurtosis.prompt: For 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, using the divisor n inside the central moments, what is the moment kurtosis?

kurtosis.title: One large observation
kurtosis.prompt: For 1, 1, 1, 1, 6, what is the moment kurtosis with divisor n, and how does it compare with 3?
kurtosis.answer: The moment kurtosis is 3.25, which is above the normal value 3.

kurtosis.title: Six numbers
kurtosis.prompt: For 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6, what is the moment kurtosis with divisor n?

lady-tasting-tea.title: Number of divisions
lady-tasting-tea.prompt: Eight cups are divided into two labelled sets of four. How many divisions are there, and what is the null probability of the correct one?
lady-tasting-tea.answer: There are 70 divisions. The null probability of the correct one is 1/70.

lady-tasting-tea.title: Three correct
lady-tasting-tea.prompt: In the eight-cup design, how many sets get exactly three of one kind right, and what is the null probability of a score at least that good?
lady-tasting-tea.answer: There are 16 such sets. Including the one perfect set gives 17/70.

lady-tasting-tea.title: Six cups
lady-tasting-tea.prompt: Six cups, three of each kind, must be split by naming a set of three. What is the null probability of a perfect score?
lady-tasting-tea.answer: There are 20 divisions, so the probability is 1/20 = 0.05.

least-absolute-deviations.title: Three-point line
least-absolute-deviations.prompt: For the points (0,0), (1,0), and (2,3), what is the sum of absolute residuals of y=1.5x?

least-absolute-deviations.title: Horizontal comparison
least-absolute-deviations.prompt: For those same three points, what is the sum of absolute residuals of the line y=0?

least-absolute-deviations.title: A second triple
least-absolute-deviations.prompt: For (0,1), (1,1), and (2,5), which line has the smaller absolute-residual sum: y=1 or y=1+2x?
least-absolute-deviations.answer: y=1+2x, with sum 2, against sum 4 for y=1.

likelihood-ratios-in-diagnostic-testing.title: Mammogram ratio
likelihood-ratios-in-diagnostic-testing.prompt: Sensitivity 0.89 and false-positive rate 0.07. What is the positive likelihood ratio?

likelihood-ratios-in-diagnostic-testing.title: Posterior probability
likelihood-ratios-in-diagnostic-testing.prompt: Prior odds about 0.003512 times a likelihood ratio of about 12.714. What is the posterior probability?

likelihood-ratios-in-diagnostic-testing.title: A simpler test
likelihood-ratios-in-diagnostic-testing.prompt: Sensitivity 0.80, false-positive rate 0.10, base rate 0.20. What are the posterior odds and the posterior probability?
likelihood-ratios-in-diagnostic-testing.answer: The posterior odds are 2 and the posterior probability is 2/3.

machine-learning.title: Reducible plus irreducible
machine-learning.prompt: A fixed fit has f(X)=10, f-hat(X)=7 and error variance 9. What is the expected squared error?

machine-learning.title: Perfect fit
machine-learning.prompt: If that same fit recovers f(X)=10 exactly, and the error variance is still 9, what is the expected squared error?

machine-learning.title: Another fixed fit
machine-learning.prompt: Now f(X)=4, f-hat(X)=1 and the error variance is 4. What is the expected squared error?

mean-absolute-percentage-error.title: Celsius percentages
mean-absolute-percentage-error.prompt: Why is a percentage forecast error a poor accuracy measure for temperature in degrees Celsius, even when every temperature is far from zero?
mean-absolute-percentage-error.answer: The zero of the Celsius scale is an arbitrary origin, not the absence of heat. Dividing an error by the temperature does not measure the miss as a share of a real level.

mean-absolute-percentage-error.title: A genuine zero
mean-absolute-percentage-error.prompt: A scored series contains a genuine zero. What happens to the mean absolute percentage error, and which part of the definition causes it?
mean-absolute-percentage-error.answer: The mean absolute percentage error is undefined or infinite, because each percentage error divides by the observation.

mean-absolute-percentage-error.title: Shared ranking
mean-absolute-percentage-error.prompt: Two methods can have the same ordering by mean absolute percentage error and by mean absolute error on one series. Why is that ordering not guaranteed on every series?
mean-absolute-percentage-error.answer: The percentage score weights each absolute error by the level of its observation. A method that misses the small observations can therefore rank differently from a method scored in the original units.

measurable-function.title: Indicators
measurable-function.prompt: Why is the indicator of a set measurable exactly when that set is an event?
measurable-function.answer: The inverse image of a Borel set under an indicator is the set itself, its complement, the whole space, or the empty set, according to whether 1 and 0 lie in the Borel set. Those four sets are events for every Borel set precisely when the indicated set is an event.

measurable-function.title: A coarse sigma-algebra
measurable-function.prompt: A sigma-algebra on a three-point set contains one singleton and the doubleton of the other two points. Why can a real function that takes three different values fail to be measurable?
measurable-function.answer: A threshold can isolate the point that the sigma-algebra does not separate from its partner. The inverse image is then a singleton that is not an event.

measurement.title: What averaging removes
measurement.prompt: Why does averaging repeated readings shrink random error and leave a shared calibration offset in place?
measurement.answer: Random errors change sign and average toward zero. A systematic error keeps one direction, so it remains in the average of the readings.

measurement.title: Two precisions
measurement.prompt: How does repeatability differ from reproducibility?
measurement.answer: Repeatability is short-term scatter with the instrument, the operator, and the setup held fixed. Reproducibility includes long-term scatter and differences across instruments or laboratories.

morans-i.title: Standardising
morans-i.prompt: Why does replacing the deviations by standardised deviations leave Moran's I unchanged?
morans-i.answer: The same scale factor appears in every product in the numerator and in the sum of squares in the denominator, so it cancels.

morans-i.title: The null centre
morans-i.prompt: Why is the reference value of Moran's I under no spatial pattern -1/(n-1) rather than zero?
morans-i.answer: Centring a finite list of values and tying them to a fixed neighbour graph forces a small negative expectation when the values are randomly reassigned. The comparison is with that expectation.

morans-i.title: Low clusters
morans-i.prompt: Why can a positive value of Moran's I describe a cluster of low values?
morans-i.answer: The products use deviations from the mean. Low next to low gives a positive product, just as high next to high does.

multilevel-model.title: Sign of the correlation
multilevel-model.prompt: Why can the within-group correlation of a random-intercept model with one variance component not be negative?
multilevel-model.answer: The covariance of two observations in the same group is the group variance, and the marginal variance is the sum of the group variance and the residual variance. A ratio of nonnegative variances is nonnegative.

multilevel-model.title: Conditional odds
multilevel-model.prompt: Why is an odds ratio from a logistic multilevel model not automatically the population-average odds ratio?
multilevel-model.answer: The coefficient is conditional on the group effect. Averaging the probability over groups is not the same operation as transforming the average of the linear predictor.

natural-experiment.title: Which condition is visible
natural-experiment.prompt: Of the three instrumental conditions proposed for an outside factor, which one can be examined in the data?
natural-experiment.answer: Only the association between the candidate instrument and the treatment. The exclusion restriction and the absence of shared causes are assumptions.

natural-experiment.title: The denominator
natural-experiment.prompt: Why is a large association between a candidate instrument and the treatment not the effect of the treatment?
natural-experiment.answer: That association is the denominator of an instrumental-variable ratio. The treatment effect is a different contrast, and it is recovered only when the instrumental conditions hold.

nonlinear-regression.title: A curved linear model
nonlinear-regression.prompt: Why is a quadratic polynomial in the predictor still fit by linear least squares?
nonlinear-regression.answer: Each power of the predictor is a known column, and the unknown coefficients stand in front of those columns. Linearity is judged in the coefficients, not in the shape of the graph.

nonlinear-regression.title: Two starts
nonlinear-regression.prompt: Why can two different starting values finish at different fitted curves?
nonlinear-regression.answer: The sum of squared errors need not have a single minimum when the mean is nonlinear in the coefficients, so the iteration can stop in different dips.

normalizing-constant.title: A ratio of heights
normalizing-constant.prompt: Why can the ratio of the posterior density at two parameter values be computed without the normalizing constant?
normalizing-constant.answer: The constant does not depend on the parameter, so it is the same at both values and cancels in the ratio.

normalizing-constant.title: An improper prior
normalizing-constant.prompt: What additional check does an improper prior require before the formal posterior is used?
normalizing-constant.answer: The integral of the unnormalised posterior must be finite. An infinite integral for the prior does not by itself make the posterior a probability density.

panel-data.title: The same people
panel-data.prompt: Why does the average of within-unit changes equal the difference of the wave means only when the panel is complete?
panel-data.answer: The algebra uses the same units at both times. Dropping a unit from one wave changes who is in that wave mean without changing the set of observed changes in the same way.

panel-data.title: Rows and histories
panel-data.prompt: Why is a panel of 20 people observed at 10 times not a sample of 200 independent residuals for a question about people?
panel-data.answer: Observations on the same person can be correlated. The independent histories are the 20 people, not the 200 rows.

pearson-distribution.title: Half the third-moment ratio
pearson-distribution.prompt: The memoir prints skewness as half of μ3/μ2^(3/2). If that printed skewness is 1/4, what is the third-moment ratio?
pearson-distribution.answer: The third-moment ratio is 1/2. The printed skewness is the gap from the mode to the mean in units of the standard deviation, and the full third-moment ratio is twice that gap.

pearson-distribution.title: Where the slope is zero
pearson-distribution.prompt: The logarithmic slope is written with the origin at the mode, so the numerator is zero at x = 0. What point of the curve does that zero mark?
pearson-distribution.answer: The mode. Moving the origin away from the mode puts a linear term back into the numerator.

pearson-distribution.title: The normal limit
pearson-distribution.prompt: A curve in the system has a vanishing third moment and μ4/μ2^2 = 3. Which named limit is that?
pearson-distribution.answer: The normal curve. In the memoir that limit is Type V, not a separate skew family.

polynomial-least-squares.title: Curved in x, linear in the coefficients
polynomial-least-squares.prompt: The mean β0 + β1 x + β2 x^2 bends in x. Why is the least-squares fit still the linear one?
polynomial-least-squares.answer: Each coefficient multiplies a column that is known once x is known. The normal equations stay linear in the coefficients. A coefficient sitting inside the function, as in an exponential rate, is the nonlinear case.

polynomial-least-squares.title: An extra free coefficient
polynomial-least-squares.prompt: A quadratic is fitted to the same points as a straight line and the residual sum of squares falls. Why is that drop expected even before anyone looks at the plot?
polynomial-least-squares.answer: The straight line is the quadratic with the square coefficient set to zero. The minimiser over a larger set of coefficients cannot have a larger residual sum of squares. The drop becomes evidence of curvature only together with the plot.

polynomial-least-squares.title: The edge of the range
polynomial-least-squares.prompt: Why is a high-degree polynomial least trustworthy near the ends of the observed range of x?
polynomial-least-squares.answer: The extra powers can swing sharply there even when the curve is calm in the middle, and a polynomial has no horizontal asymptote to level off.

posterior-probability.title: A sampling probability is not yet posterior
posterior-probability.prompt: The data have sampling probability 1/2 under one explanation and 1/6 under another. Why is 1/2 not already the posterior probability of the first explanation?
posterior-probability.answer: Sampling probabilities need not add to one across explanations. The posterior multiplies each by its prior and divides by the sum of those products.

posterior-probability.title: A prior of zero
posterior-probability.prompt: An explanation is given prior probability 0, and the data are very likely under it. What is its posterior probability, when the posterior is defined?
posterior-probability.answer: Zero. The likelihood does not create mass outside the support of the prior.

posterior-probability.title: A single point of a continuous parameter
posterior-probability.prompt: A continuous posterior density is positive at θ = 1/2. What is the posterior probability of the single point θ = 1/2?
posterior-probability.answer: Zero. A posterior probability is the mass of a set, and a continuous distribution gives every single point mass zero. The mass of an interval around 1/2 can still be large.

probability-interpretations.title: Arithmetic the readings share
probability-interpretations.prompt: A symmetry assignment and a long-run frequency can disagree about the number written for heads. Which rules do they still share?
probability-interpretations.answer: The probability of the sample space is 1, the empty event has probability 0, the complement subtracts from 1, and incompatible events add. The union of any two events subtracts the intersection once.

probability-interpretations.title: One launch, no reference set
probability-interpretations.prompt: A strict frequency account requires a long sequence of comparable repetitions. What does that account withhold for a single rocket launch that is not treated as one of a class?
probability-interpretations.answer: A probability for that launch. The uncertainty reading can still assign one. The axioms do not choose between those readings.

probability-interpretations.title: A bent coin
probability-interpretations.prompt: The two faces of a coin are declared equally likely, and the coin is then found to be bent. Which part of the assignment has failed?
probability-interpretations.answer: The symmetry judgement. The axioms do not detect that the faces were not exchangeable. They detect an assignment that contradicts itself, such as nonnegative weights that do not add to one.

random-error.title: What a correction can remove
random-error.prompt: Every reading of a rod is 0.2 cm high because the zero is wrong, and the readings also scatter from trial to trial. Which part can a correction remove?
random-error.answer: The systematic shift of 0.2 cm. The scatter that changes direction from trial to trial is the random error, and a single correction does not remove it.

random-error.title: The same differences, two statements
random-error.prompt: Differences among several instruments are a random effect when the uncertainty statement covers an instrument drawn at random from the batch. What are those differences when the statement covers one named instrument?
random-error.answer: The bias of that instrument relative to the batch. The analysis is then a bias analysis, and a bias can be corrected in a way a random error cannot.

random-error.title: A residual is a different gap
random-error.prompt: A fitted mean is subtracted from an observation. Why is that gap not the random error of a repeated measurement against a fixed reference?
random-error.answer: The residual is the gap between an estimate and the observation, and the estimate was computed from the observations. The random error is the chance part of the gap between a measurement and the reference value.

ranking.title: Why the ranks sum to the triangular number
ranking.prompt: Four distinct values are ranked 1 through 4, with no ties. What is the sum of the ranks, and why does a tie that is given average ranks keep the same sum?
ranking.answer: The sum is 10, because the ranks are the first four positive integers. Average ranks share the places that those integers would have occupied, so the total is unchanged.

ranking.title: A tie for first
ranking.prompt: Two observations tie for the two best places when rank 1 is the smallest. Why is each given 1.5 rather than both given 1?
ranking.answer: The places 1 and 2 are shared. Their average is 1.5. Giving both the rank 1 would drop the sum of all ranks below the sum for an untied ranking.

ranking.title: What the raw scale loses
ranking.prompt: Spearman's coefficient is computed from ranks rather than from the raw measurements. What feature of the raw scale does that discard?
ranking.answer: The spacing between the values. Only the order, and the average places of ties, remain. A strictly increasing transformation of the measurements leaves the ranks unchanged.

raw-data.title: What the mean can no longer answer
raw-data.prompt: Five reaction times are replaced by their mean. Which comparison among the five times can that mean still support?
raw-data.answer: None. The mean is one number. Which time was longest, and whether two times were equal, is no longer in the summary.

raw-data.title: A row is a case
raw-data.prompt: A spreadsheet of loans has one row per loan and a column for the interest rate. What is lost if only the column of rates is kept?
raw-data.answer: The link between each rate and the other variables of that same loan, such as income and state. The rate is still a number. It is no longer the rate of a case.

raw-data.title: A correction is not a reduction
raw-data.prompt: A recorded time of 16 seconds is later judged to be a mis-keyed 10. Is that change a summary, or a change to the record?
raw-data.answer: A change to the record. Data reduction replaces several numbers by fewer numbers. Correcting a keying error changes what was written down.

resampling-statistics.title: A hole the resamples keep
resampling-statistics.prompt: The original sample misses an entire region of the population. What do bootstrap samples drawn from it say about that region?
resampling-statistics.answer: Nothing new. Every resample is built from the original observations, so the missing region stays missing. The bootstrap spread describes the sample that was drawn.

resampling-statistics.title: Zero bias is not a small variance
resampling-statistics.prompt: The sample mean has jackknife bias zero. Does that make the mean a precise estimator?
resampling-statistics.answer: No. Jackknife bias zero means the leave-one-out correction does not shift the estimate. The mean can still have a large variance. The bias correction is aimed at a term of order 1/n, not at the spread.

resampling-statistics.title: Two different refits
resampling-statistics.prompt: Cross-validation and the bootstrap both recompute something from the sample. What does each one score?
resampling-statistics.answer: Cross-validation scores observations held out of the fit, and estimates prediction error. The bootstrap refits the statistic on resamples of the whole sample, and estimates the sampling variability of that statistic.

robust-statistics.title: Absolute deviations
robust-statistics.prompt: For 1, 2, 3, 4 and 20, what are the sums of absolute deviations from the mean 6 and from the median 3?
robust-statistics.answer: The sums are 28 at the mean and 21 at the median.

robust-statistics.title: Squared deviations
robust-statistics.prompt: For the same five numbers, what are the sums of squared deviations from 6 and from 3?
robust-statistics.answer: The sums are 250 at the mean and 295 at the median.

robust-statistics.title: One wild point
robust-statistics.prompt: For 5, 5, 5, 5 and 100, what are the mean and the sum of absolute deviations from the median?
robust-statistics.answer: The mean is 24 and the sum of absolute deviations from the median 5 is 95.

rounding.title: Proportional shares
rounding.prompt: The exact shares 14.25, 7.5, 4.5 and 3.75 are each rounded half-up to an integer. What is the sum of the rounded shares?
rounding.answer: The rounded shares are 14, 8, 5 and 4, and they sum to 31.

rounding.title: A printed margin
rounding.prompt: Two printed proportions are 0.851 and 0.150. By how much does their sum exceed 1?
rounding.answer: Their sum is 1.001, which exceeds 1 by 0.001.

rounding.title: Three numbers
rounding.prompt: Round 2.5, 2.5 and 3.2 half-up. What is the sum of the rounded values?
rounding.answer: The rounded values are 3, 3 and 3, and they sum to 9.

sampling.title: Equally likely subsets
sampling.prompt: A simple random sample of 2 units is drawn from 6. How many equally likely samples are there?

sampling.title: Larger population
sampling.prompt: The population has 10 units and the sample size is still 2. How many equally likely samples are there?

scientific-control.title: Two means
scientific-control.prompt: Drug changes sum to 54 over 6 patients and placebo changes sum to 18 over 6. What is the contrast of means?
scientific-control.answer: The means are 9 and 3, so the contrast is 6.

scientific-control.title: Extra placebo
scientific-control.prompt: The placebo changes sum to 22 over 7 patients and the drug mean stays 9. What is the placebo mean?

secondary-data.title: Recorded risk
secondary-data.prompt: A file of 240 admissions records 30 falls. What is the recorded risk?

secondary-data.title: Found admissions
secondary-data.prompt: Twelve further admissions are added, 3 of them with a fall. What is the new recorded risk as a count?
secondary-data.answer: The file has 33 falls among 252 admissions.

spearman-s-rank-correlation-coefficient.title: Mild disagreement
spearman-s-rank-correlation-coefficient.prompt: Rank differences are 0, 0, -1, and 1, so the squared differences sum to 2, and n = 4. What is the coefficient?

spearman-s-rank-correlation-coefficient.title: Complete reversal
spearman-s-rank-correlation-coefficient.prompt: The squared rank differences for a complete reversal of four ranks sum to 20. What is the coefficient?

statistical-dispersion.title: Five numbers
statistical-dispersion.prompt: For 2, 4, 4, 7 and 8, what are the sample variance with divisor n−1, the average absolute deviation from the mean, and the range?
statistical-dispersion.answer: The sample variance is 6, the average absolute deviation is 2, and the range is 6.

statistical-dispersion.title: Seven family sizes
statistical-dispersion.prompt: For 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3 and 6, what is the range, and what is the average absolute deviation from the mean as a fraction?
statistical-dispersion.answer: The range is 6. The average absolute deviation is 76/49.

statistical-model.title: Error and parameters
statistical-model.prompt: In the equation Y = β0 + β1 X + ε, which symbol is the unobservable random error, and which symbols are the unknown parameters?
statistical-model.answer: The error is ε. The parameters are β0 and β1.

statistical-model.title: A squared predictor
statistical-model.prompt: Does squaring the explanatory variable make Y = β0 + β1 X + β2 X^2 + ε nonlinear in the coefficients?
statistical-model.answer: No. The equation is still linear in β0, β1 and β2. The square is on X.

statistical-model.title: A different residual
statistical-model.prompt: The fitted line is ŷ = 1 + 2x. At x = 3 the observation is y = 10. What is the residual?
statistical-model.answer: The fitted value is 7, so the residual is 3.

statistical-survey.title: Sample proportion
statistical-survey.prompt: Of 50 drawn households, 35 have a working alarm, from a city of 1000. What is the sample proportion?

statistical-survey.title: Larger draw
statistical-survey.prompt: Of 80 households, 60 have a working alarm. What are the sample proportion and the sampling fraction out of 1000?
statistical-survey.answer: The sample proportion is 0.75 and the sampling fraction is 0.08.

statistician.title: A statistic and a decision
statistician.prompt: The mean of a set of district birth counts is a statistic. The choice of which districts belong in the total is not. What is the difference?
statistician.answer: A statistic is a number computed from the sample by a rule that does not contain an unknown parameter. Choosing the districts decides what the collection is for, before that rule is applied.

statistician.title: What one mean hides
statistician.prompt: A report of district births gives only the mean. Which feature of the district counts can that single number not show?
statistician.answer: It cannot show how unequal the districts are. The spread across districts is a separate part of the description.

statistician.title: The broader definition
statistician.prompt: Under the broader official-statistics reading, a survey manager counts as a statistician. What do the theoretical statistician, the survey methodologist, the subject-matter specialist, the information technologist, and the survey manager have in common?
statistician.answer: Each contributes to getting statistics and data to users. The common point is the delivered product, not a single degree.

supervised-learning.title: Training error of zero
supervised-learning.prompt: One-nearest neighbour reproduces every training label, so the training error is zero. Why is that not an estimate of the error at a new feature?
supervised-learning.answer: Each training point is its own nearest neighbour, so the score uses the labels twice. A new feature is a different query, and the training error does not measure overlap between the classes.

supervised-learning.title: Logistic regression
supervised-learning.prompt: Why is logistic regression supervised learning even though the method has regression in its name?
supervised-learning.answer: The training cases carry a qualitative response. The fitted probability is a means to a class, so the response supervises the fit.

supervised-learning.title: Labels removed
supervised-learning.prompt: If the labels on a supervised training sample are thrown away, what remains and what is lost?
supervised-learning.answer: The distances among the features remain. The predicted label does not, because there is no response left to return.

survey-methodology.title: A complete response from a short frame
survey-methodology.prompt: Every person who was drawn replies, but the frame omitted a whole class of the target population. Which survey error remains?
survey-methodology.answer: Coverage error remains. Non-response has been removed, and the omitted class was never eligible to be drawn.

survey-methodology.title: A clearer question
survey-methodology.prompt: Why does rewriting a question so that respondents understand it fail to shrink sampling error?
survey-methodology.answer: Questionnaire error and sampling error are different sources. Wording changes the measurement, not the way the sample was selected.

survey-methodology.title: When non-response is an error
survey-methodology.prompt: A survey has refusals. When do those refusals create non-response error, rather than merely a smaller sample?
survey-methodology.answer: When the people who decline differ, in a way that matters to the study, from the people who answer.

systematic-error.title: More repetitions
systematic-error.prompt: A balance has a constant offset. Why does taking more readings fail to remove that offset from the average?
systematic-error.answer: The variance of the average falls as the sample grows, but the expected value of the average stays a fixed distance from the standard. The average settles on the wrong value more firmly.

systematic-error.title: No reference standard
systematic-error.prompt: Why can the scatter of a series of readings, with no reference standard, not estimate the systematic offset?
systematic-error.answer: The deviations from the mean sum to zero. They estimate the random scale, and they say nothing about a shift that is common to every reading.

systematic-error.title: Two systematic errors
systematic-error.prompt: The bias of an estimator and a miscalibrated instrument are both systematic errors. What is being repeated in each case?
systematic-error.answer: Estimator bias is a gap in expectation under a sampling model. A calibration offset is a property of one measurement procedure. The remedies differ because the repeated thing differs.

systematic-sampling.title: Not every subset
systematic-sampling.prompt: Why is a systematic sample with interval r not a simple random sample of the same size?
systematic-sampling.answer: Simple random sampling gives every subset of that size the same probability. Systematic sampling can produce only the r arithmetic progressions with difference r.

systematic-sampling.title: A repeating trait
systematic-sampling.prompt: The list order cycles with a period that divides the sampling interval. What can go wrong?
systematic-sampling.answer: Every selected unit can land on the same phase of the cycle, so the sample repeats one part of the pattern instead of moving through it.

systematic-sampling.title: The start
systematic-sampling.prompt: The interval is fixed and the first unit is whichever line looks convenient. Why has the draw left the random methods?
systematic-sampling.answer: The interval alone is not the randomisation. The random methods require a random start. A convenient start is an arbitrary selection.

tail.title: Two regions
tail.prompt: For a continuous distribution, why do the lower-tail and upper-tail probabilities at the same cutoff add to 1?
tail.answer: The outcome is either at or below the cutoff or above it, and those two events exhaust the probability.

tail.title: The sign of skewness
tail.prompt: A skewness coefficient is positive. Which tail is long relative to the other?
tail.answer: The right tail is long relative to the left tail. The distribution is skewed right.

tail.title: Shape and probability
tail.prompt: A histogram trails off to the right. Why is that not yet a numerical value of P(X > c)?
tail.answer: A long right tail names a shape. A tail probability needs a cutoff and either a distribution or an empirical proportion beyond that cutoff.

true-value.title: Tight scatter
true-value.prompt: Repeated measurements cluster tightly around their own average, and that average is not the reference. Has the procedure hit the true value?
true-value.answer: No. Tight scatter is precision around the procedure's average. Accuracy also includes the offset from the true value, and that offset can be large while the scatter is small.

true-value.title: When the average matches
true-value.prompt: When is the average of the measurements equal to the true value?
true-value.answer: When the remaining errors happen to cancel, or when one is speaking of the expected value of an unbiased procedure. The average is otherwise an estimate of the true value.

true-value.title: A category code
true-value.prompt: Why does a code for a category not have a true value in the metrological sense?
true-value.answer: The metrological true value is a quantity that repeated measurement is trying to recover. A category code is not that kind of quantity.

uncertainty.title: A small standard error
uncertainty.prompt: An estimator has a very small standard error. Why can the target still be the wrong one?
uncertainty.answer: The standard error describes scatter under the sampling scheme and the model that were used. A biased procedure can be precise about the wrong number, because bias and precision answer different questions.

uncertainty.title: A curved residual plot
uncertainty.prompt: A residual plot from a fitted line shows a curve. What does that add to an uncertainty statement that quoted only the scatter of the observations?
uncertainty.answer: The curve is a sign that the line was the wrong shape. That leftover pattern is model uncertainty, which a scatter computed under the line does not include.

uncertainty.title: A weak denominator
uncertainty.prompt: An instrumental-variable estimate is a ratio whose denominator is a weak association. Why is the point estimate not the uncertainty?
uncertainty.answer: The uncertainty is the width of the set of plausible values. A weak denominator inflates that width, so the interval and the point estimate are different objects.

unsupervised-learning.title: No training error
unsupervised-learning.prompt: Why is there no training error, of the supervised kind, that goes to zero by memorising the data in an unsupervised analysis?
unsupervised-learning.answer: No response was recorded, so there is no label to memorise and no loss on a response to drive to zero. The procedure returns a description, such as a partition or a direction.

unsupervised-learning.title: A later response
unsupervised-learning.prompt: Why might the direction that carries most of the variance fail to predict a response collected later?
unsupervised-learning.answer: Principal components ignore any response. A low-variance coordinate can be the one that predicts.

unsupervised-learning.title: A change of units
unsupervised-learning.prompt: The features are measured in arbitrary units, and one coordinate is multiplied by ten before the variances are computed. What question do the new fractions answer?
unsupervised-learning.answer: They answer a question about the units. A variance or a distance from a badly scaled feature describes the scale, not the subject.

regression-analysis.title: Several predictors, still linear
regression-analysis.prompt: A mean uses three predictors and is linear in the coefficients. Why is that still linear regression, even if the picture against one raw predictor is not a straight line?
regression-analysis.answer: Linearity is judged in the coefficients. Each predictor multiplies its own coefficient. A power of one predictor is still a linear term of that kind. A coefficient sitting inside the mean function is the nonlinear case.

regression-analysis.title: How squaring charges a large residual
regression-analysis.prompt: One residual is 4 and another is 2. By what factor does squared error charge the larger residual, relative to the smaller, and how does that compare with absolute error?
regression-analysis.answer: Squared error charges 16 against 4, a factor of four. Absolute error charges 4 against 2, a factor of two. The two criteria fit different lines.

regression-analysis.title: A slope is not yet an intervention
regression-analysis.prompt: A fitted slope is positive inside the observed range of a predictor. What further condition is required before that slope is read as the change from setting the predictor to a new value?
regression-analysis.answer: The design has to support that intervention. The fit is a summary of the sample. An observational association can run through a confounder, and the algebra does not name it.

survival-analysis.title: A hazard above one
survival-analysis.prompt: A hazard equals 2 per year. Why is that not a probability of death?
survival-analysis.answer: The hazard is a conditional rate per unit time. The probability of an event in a short interval is about the hazard times the length of the interval, and the rate itself need not be smaller than one.

survival-analysis.title: Sick patients leave
survival-analysis.prompt: The sickest patients drop out of a study early, and the analysis ignores why they left. What happens to the estimated survival?
survival-analysis.answer: The estimate tends to overstate survival. Independent censoring fails when the event time and the censoring time are dependent given the features.

survival-analysis.title: Shared shocks
survival-analysis.prompt: Two components must both work, and they share a cause of failure. Why is the system reliability not the square of one component reliability?
survival-analysis.answer: The product rule is for independent components. A shared cause makes the event times dependent, so the joint reliability is not the product.

bayesian-statistics.title: The three steps
bayesian-statistics.prompt: What are the three steps in the outline of a Bayesian analysis?
bayesian-statistics.answer: Write a joint probability model, condition on the observed data, and check whether the model and its conclusions hold up.

bayesian-statistics.title: Reading an interval
bayesian-statistics.prompt: Inside the model, how is an interval that holds posterior probability 0.95 read?
bayesian-statistics.answer: As an interval that has probability 0.95 of containing the unknown.

bayesian-statistics.title: Where the normal approximation stops
bayesian-statistics.prompt: Why can the large-sample normal approximation to a posterior fail when the true value sits on the boundary of the parameter space?
bayesian-statistics.answer: The Taylor expansion is cut off in some directions, so the limiting shape need not be normal.

estimation-theory.title: Target
estimation-theory.prompt: A sample mean of 4 and a sample variance of 8/3 are computed from the same four numbers. What distinguishes them?
estimation-theory.answer: They are different functions of the sample, aimed at different population quantities.

estimation-theory.title: Estimator and parameter
estimation-theory.prompt: Why is the number 4 not itself the population mean?
estimation-theory.answer: It is a function of one sample. The population mean is the quantity the sample mean is aimed at.

probability-theory.title: Intersections from unions
probability-theory.prompt: A σ-field is closed under complements and under countable unions. Why is it also closed under countable intersections?
probability-theory.answer: The intersection of the sets Ai is the complement of the union of their complements. Both of those operations stay inside the collection.

probability-theory.title: The empty event
probability-theory.prompt: A probability measure satisfies P(Ω) = 1 and is countably additive. What is P(∅), and why?
probability-theory.answer: Zero. The sample space and the empty set are disjoint and their union is the sample space, so P(Ω) = P(Ω) + P(∅).

probability-theory.title: A countable space
probability-theory.prompt: The outcomes of a countable space are given nonnegative weights that sum to 1. What is the probability of an event?
probability-theory.answer: The sum of the weights of the outcomes inside the event. An uncountable space cannot give every point the same positive weight, because that sum would not be a probability.

multivariate-statistics.title: Variances and a correlation
multivariate-statistics.prompt: Why can two marginal variances be equal and positive while the correlation of the same two coordinates is negative?
multivariate-statistics.answer: The variances are sums of squares of deviations. The correlation also uses the products of paired deviations, and those products can be negative.

multivariate-statistics.title: Total variation
multivariate-statistics.prompt: Why does a principal-component decomposition not increase the total variation of the coordinates?
multivariate-statistics.answer: The component variances sum to the trace of the covariance matrix, which is the sum of the original variances.

multivariate-statistics.title: Checking a summary
multivariate-statistics.prompt: Why is an unsupervised summary harder to check than a classifier?
multivariate-statistics.answer: A classifier has a response that can be scored on cases the rule did not use. An unsupervised summary has no response to get wrong.

structural-equation-modelling.title: A covariance p-value
structural-equation-modelling.prompt: A structural equation model has a large p-value on its covariance chi-square. What has been checked, and what has not?
structural-equation-modelling.answer: The implied covariances are not far from the sample covariances under the fitted linear structure. The test does not establish that the arrows are interventions.

structural-equation-modelling.title: Two structural equations
structural-equation-modelling.prompt: How does a nonparametric structural equation differ from a factor loading estimated from a covariance matrix?
structural-equation-modelling.answer: The nonparametric equation writes each variable as a function of its graph parents and an error, and an intervention substitutes a value into that function. A loading is a parameter of a measurement model fit to second moments.

structural-equation-modelling.title: Non-normal standard errors
structural-equation-modelling.prompt: Continuous indicators are skewed, and the model is fit by ordinary maximum likelihood. What can go wrong with the usual standard errors even if the point estimates stay consistent?
structural-equation-modelling.answer: The usual standard errors can be too small, so a coefficient is declared different from zero too often. The chi-square can also be too large.

standard-score.title: Below the mean
standard-score.prompt: A distribution has mean 55 and standard deviation 5. What is the standard score of an observation equal to 40?

standard-score.title: At the mean
standard-score.prompt: What is the standard score of an observation that equals the mean of its distribution?

standard-score.title: Which is more unusual
standard-score.prompt: One observation has standard score 0.4 and another has standard score -1.2, on distributions of similar shape. Which is more unusual, and why?
standard-score.answer: The observation with standard score -1.2 is more unusual, because the absolute value 1.2 is larger than 0.4.

test-statistic.title: Null standard error
test-statistic.prompt: In a test of a single proportion, why is the standard error computed from the null value rather than from the sample proportion?
test-statistic.answer: The reference distribution is the distribution of the statistic when the null is true, so the standardisation uses that null value.

test-statistic.title: Three different numbers
test-statistic.prompt: A proportion test reports a sample proportion, a Z statistic, and a p-value. What does each one measure?
test-statistic.answer: The sample proportion is the estimate. The Z statistic is the estimate minus the null value, divided by the null standard error. The p-value is a tail probability of that statistic under the null.

test-statistic.title: After the fact
test-statistic.prompt: Several comparisons are examined and the most extreme statistic is then treated as the pre-specified test. What has changed about the null probability of rejection?
test-statistic.answer: The rejection probability is now the probability for the search, not the probability tabulated for one pre-specified statistic.
